newsitem.title: UK: French investors hunt for yield in foreign issuers.
newsitem.headline: French investors hunt for yield in foreign issuers.

text.p: Cash-rich French bond investors, taking the view French yields might have reached their lows, will be particularly choosy about where to put their money for the next few months, syndicate managers said on Wednesday.
"Earlier this year, investors would buy anything that had a fair price in order to get exposure to the bull market," said a syndicate manager at a French bank.
"Now, they think the market is going sideways, and the only way to get them in is to offer something which is too good to refuse," he said.
This month, about 6.7 billion franc ($1.3 billion) Eurobonds will be redeemed, and a further 11.5 billion francs will mature in December, according to Capital DATA Bondware.
In October, 40 billion francs worth of coupon payments on government debt were made, and some is still held in cash, traders said. Further coupon payments were due in November.
"French investors think yields are quite low, and they are not convinced bond markets will continue to rally," the French bank official said.
As a result, "they either buy bonds from lower-rated borrowers that give extra yield or paper that is priced a few basis points too cheaply," he said.
In terms of extra yield, some investors were looking at foreign borrowers in French francs, an area attracting many foreign issuers because of the favourable swap opportunities through arbitrage.
"All issuers are looking at the franc market, but there are still only a handful of firm deals in the pipeline," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank in Paris.
Borrowers planning for European economic and monetary union, which is due to take place in 1999, are also tapping the franc sector to establish a following among investors there.
The European Investment bank and Suedwestdeutsche Landesbank said the franc bonds launched in October were part of a strategy to set benchmarks in all major European currencies before EMU.
But EMU pressures are also feeding through to underwriters.

"A lot of people who have been marginally involved in French francs are now waking up to the fact it is a large market and they want to place themselves there ahead of 1999," said a new issues trader in Paris.
"There are a lot of extraneous factors motivating issuance at the moment, which have nothing to do with fundamentals of the market. We may have a very busy few months ahead," he said.
Nevertheless, that type of interest in the franc sector should be encouraging to investors who still favour the foreign borrowers offering more yield over domestic issues.

For example, "non-French triple-A credits yield 12-15 basis points over OATs (French government bonds), whereas CNA's (Caisse Nationale des Autoroutes), recent 12-year bond came at nine basis points over," a Paris-based syndicate manager said.
Meanwhile, French double-A rated names were trading between two and five basis points below similarly-rated foreign credits, he added.

French insurance companies, who are cash-rich at the moment, tend to buy longer-dated paper and are very driven by absolute yield levels. And now that 10-year French government bond yields were below six percent, some might buy Eurobonds instead, a trader said.
Upcoming deals include a 1.5 billion French franc bond for Australian company Telstra and a jumbo deal for up to 5.0 billion francs for U.S. agency Federal National Mortgage Association.
Norddeutsche Landesbank said it would issue a 2.0 billion franc deal before the end of 1996 and Italy's Crediop was also holding investor presentations.
Investors are also partial to foreign borrowers because those issues can help diversify their portfolios.
